title: Learn how fasting works (Sawm)
whyMatters: Fasting through the month of Ramadan is one of the five pillars of Islam. From dawn to sunset Muslims go without food, drink, and other physical needs, as worship, as self-discipline, and to feel some of what people with less feel all year. It teaches patience and gratitude, and it pulls you closer to Allah. Ask around and most Muslims will name Ramadan as the best month of their year: company every evening, time to think, and a faith that sits closer than usual. Even if Ramadan is months off, learning how fasting works now means it will not catch you cold.

subSteps: Fasting is commanded in the Quran: 'O you who believe, fasting is prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you, so that you may become mindful of God.' (2:183)
It builds taqwa (God-consciousness), an awareness of Allah in whatever you are doing.
It gives you a real feel for hunger, and for the people who live with it.
It is a month for extra prayer, more Quran, and a general reset.
Breaking the fast together (iftar) does a lot for how close a community feels.

exactActions.text: Learn the basic rules of fasting
subSteps: The fast begins at Fajr (dawn) and ends at Maghrib (sunset).
During fasting hours you keep off food, drink including water, and marital intimacy.
You eat a pre-dawn meal called suhoor before Fajr prayer. Do not skip it, because it carries your energy through the day.
You break the fast at sunset with a meal called iftar. The Prophet (peace be upon him) recommended breaking fast with dates and water.
Each day's fast needs a fresh intention (niyyah), which is just a thought in your heart that you are fasting for Allah.

exactActions.text: Know who is exempt from fasting
subSteps: Travelers may postpone the fast and make the days up later.
Anyone who is ill, or has a medical condition that makes fasting dangerous, is exempt.
Pregnant or breastfeeding women may be exempt if fasting puts them at risk.
Women do not fast during menstruation, and they make those days up afterwards.
Older people who cannot fast may feed a person in need for each day instead.
Children are not required to fast, though many start easing into it.
You do not have to wait for Ramadan to find out what fasting is like.
The Prophet (peace be upon him) encouraged fasting on Mondays and Thursdays.
Fast for one day and see how it goes.
Eat a good suhoor, drink well before and after fasting hours, and break the fast gently.
Afterwards, notice what it did to your attention and your gratitude.
Ramadan follows the Islamic lunar calendar, so the dates shift each year.
The month starts with the sighting of the new moon.
Masjids hold special nightly prayers called Tarawih through Ramadan.
Many masjids put on community iftars, which are among the easiest events for a new Muslim to walk into.
Ramadan ends with Eid al-Fitr, a holiday of prayers, food, and gifts.

timeEstimate: One day for a trial fast. Ramadan itself is a full month, once a year

obstacles.problem: I don't think I can go all day without eating or drinking
obstacles.solution: This is the most common worry and it makes sense. The body adapts better than you would guess. A solid suhoor with slow carbohydrates, protein, and water carries you a long way. The first few days are the hardest and then it eases off. If fasting is new to you, try shorter voluntary fasts first. In winter the days are short, roughly ten hours in Toronto. And if your health genuinely will not allow it, Islam has alternatives for you.

obstacles.problem: I have to fast while working or studying
obstacles.solution: Millions of Muslims fast through full work and school weeks. Plan your meals, because a decent suhoor does most of the work. Keep busy during the day so food stays off your mind. Plenty of people find they focus better while fasting. Tell a colleague you trust if you need a small accommodation, like a quiet spot for a short prayer break. It turns out to be more manageable than it sounds.

Your health comes first, and Islam exempts anyone whose health would be harmed by fasting. Talk to your doctor before you fast if you have diabetes, take medication that needs food, or live with any chronic condition. If you cannot fast, you can feed a person in need for each day missed (fidyah). There is nothing shameful in that, because it is the guidance of the Quran itself.

obstacles.problem: My family doesn't fast and meal times are awkward
obstacles.solution: You can fast whether or not anyone around you does. Make your own suhoor and iftar. If a family meal lands during fasting hours, sit with them for the company and leave the food. Many converts find their family gets curious and supportive once they understand what the fast means to you, and some will try a day themselves.

obstacles.problem: I'm not sure if I'm doing it right
obstacles.solution: The fast is valid as long as you intended it for Allah, you kept off food and drink from Fajr to Maghrib, and you are not in an exempt category. If you eat or drink because you simply forgot, the fast still stands, and the Prophet (peace be upon him) called that a provision from Allah. Do not overthink it. Your sincerity is the part that matters.

tinyVersion: Fasting means no food or drink from dawn to sunset. Try one day and see how it goes. If your health rules it out, that is fine, and Islam gives you another way to take part.
unlocksNext: Fasting shows you what Islamic self-discipline actually feels like. Next comes character, which is where most of living as a Muslim really happens.
